venues.d: A hushed vertical sanctuary in the Crown Building — the city, finally, on silent.
The Upper East Side's most glamorous house — the only New York hotel on the world list.
Old-New-York grandeur with a cabaret in the basement — the city's most storied address.
A Beaux-Arts landmark on Fifth, with the group's famous precision and a rooftop bar.
Park-and-skyline views from on high at Columbus Circle — the group's calm, precise flagship.

venues.n: Four Seasons Hotel New York Downtown
venues.d: The surest hands in Lower Manhattan — service you never have to think about.
The house that invented the butler — Astor-era Beaux-Arts splendour off Fifth Avenue.

venues.n: The Ritz-Carlton New York, Central Park
venues.d: Park-facing tradition on Central Park South — grand, gracious, and reliably excellent.
Crystal-chandelier glamour opposite MoMA — a jewel-box of a hotel, and it knows it.
A calm, contemporary tower on Billionaires' Row — quiet luxury, beautifully run.

venues.n: The Towers at Lotte New York Palace
venues.d: A hotel-within-a-hotel in a Gilded-Age courtyard mansion — the exclusive Towers wing.
A members'-club hotel in a landmark ferry terminal — Italian glamour on the water's edge.
Firmdale's English-country-house colour dropped into the heart of SoHo.
A joyful, art-filled Firmdale house a whisper from Fifth Avenue and Central Park.
A discreet townhouse hotel of wood fires and fresh flowers — old-money calm.
Robert De Niro's Tribeca hideaway — a warm, worldly house with a lantern-lit pool.
A gilded mansion-and-tower debut — maximalist, romantic, the talk of NoMad.
Parisian glamour on the Hudson side of Tribeca — the Champs-Élysées, restaged downtown.
A sleek new-build in the Hudson Yards district — polished, contemporary, well-run.
Firmdale's downtown debut — the same fearless colour, now in Tribeca.
A landmark 1912 bank turned design-led hotel — the coolest room downtown.
Nature-led calm steps from Central Park — reclaimed wood, living walls, easy comfort.
A breathtaking nine-storey Victorian atrium downtown — history with a modern pulse.
A quietly elegant house in the old financial heart — a calm downtown residence.
The original SoHo loft hotel — spare, timeless, and endlessly cool.
A dimly-lit, velvet-and-candles downtown classic — romantic and a little bohemian.
A relaxed, downtown-cool house on the Lower East Side — effortless and unpretentious.
A tall, contemporary Ritz-Carlton with a rooftop over the Empire State Building.
A refined Upper East Side residence, newly reborn under Corinthia — quiet, gracious calm.
The London members'-club hotel's first New York address — buzzy and of-the-moment.
The most legendary bohemian hotel in America — reborn, and steeped in its own myth.
The best Manhattan-skyline view in the city — from the Brooklyn side of the river.
A converted Williamsburg factory with a rooftop bar and the skyline across the water.
A design-led, art-filled house in brownstone Brooklyn — relaxed and creative.
Understated elegance in a landmark clock tower over Madison Square Park.
A one-of-a-kind Japanese-crafted penthouse above the Greenwich — the city's most private suite.

venues.n: Trump International Hotel & Tower New York
venues.d: Full Central Park frontage at Columbus Circle — big windows, big views.
Daniel Humm's plant-based three-star — the most talked-about fine-dining room in America.
Eric Ripert's temple to seafood — three stars held for decades, and never a slip.
Thomas Keller's New York flagship — a hushed room over Central Park, at the summit.
Yim Jungsik's modern Korean — the cuisine reimagined at the very highest level.
The city's newest three-star — a revered Tokyo master's edomae omakase.
The Parks' Korean tasting counter — named the best restaurant in North America.
Masa Takayama's austere, extravagant sushi — still among the costliest meals in America.
Daniel Boulud's grand French dining room — the Upper East Side's most elegant table.
Jean-Georges Vongerichten's flagship — light, precise French with a park view.
Refined American cooking overlooking MoMA's sculpture garden — art on both sides of the glass.
Alsatian-French cooking of real soul, overlooking Bryant Park.
The city's benchmark for Nordic cooking — cool, clean, and quietly luxurious.
Fredrik Berselius's Nordic tasting menu in a candlelit Williamsburg townhouse.
An intimate Tribeca counter of exacting, seasonal tasting menus.
A tasting menu high in a landmark 1930s skyscraper — the view is part of the meal.
A French-Japanese two-star that arrived fully formed — precise and personal.
An intense, seafood-led counter — one of the city's most serious tasting experiences.
A refined Korean tasting menu, newly elevated to two stars — quiet, considered, exact.
A hinoki-wood counter of pure edomae craft — sushi as meditation.
A serene kaiseki counter hidden behind a tea room — Japan, faithfully rendered.
The only Indian restaurant in America to hold a Michelin star — South India, uncompromised.
Andrew Carmellini's grand, romantic Italian-French room inside The Fifth Avenue Hotel.
Italian-American cooking with a New-York swagger, in the landmark Puck Building.
A love letter to Emilia-Romagna — the city's most wanted pasta.
A beautiful, candlelit ode to classical French cooking in the heart of SoHo.
James Kent's downtown room — inventive, generous, and consistently excellent.

venues.n: The Dining Room at Gramercy Tavern
venues.d: A New York institution — seasonal American cooking of unwavering grace.
A Korean steakhouse of real refinement — the butcher's counter meets the tasting menu.
Daniel Boulud's soaring, garden-like room of vegetable- and seafood-led French cooking.
Daniel Boulud's warm, seasonal café — refined French with an easy grace.
A joyful, generous omakase from a Jiro-trained master — sushi with a smile.
Modern Northern Mexican cooking that earned a star within a year of opening.
Amanda Cohen's pioneering vegetable tasting menu — the case for vegetables, made joyfully.
A wine bar that quietly became one of the country's best restaurants.
A newly-starred Chinatown room bringing quiet French finesse to a downtown corner.
A caviar-and-seafood tasting counter of great luxury — newly starred.
A precise new Japanese counter that earned its star straight out of the gate.
An intimate tasting menu hidden behind an art-gallery door — French with a Brazilian pulse.
A tiny yakitori counter of great purity — every part of the bird over charcoal.
New York's oldest French bistro, lovingly revived — a piece of the city's soul.
The West Village trattoria everyone wants a table at — simple, perfect, always full.
Unapologetic, rustic Indian cooking that pulls no punches — a love letter to the regions.
Vikas Khanna's ode to Indian country-club dining — glamorous, generous, joyful.
Modern Indian cooking with a light, contemporary hand — Bib-listed and easy to love.
Warm, well-made Indian cooking that quietly earned the inspectors' nod.
A serene, shoes-off Korean temple restaurant — entirely vegetarian, and quietly special.
A glamorous Korean fried-chicken-and-Champagne room — serious fun, seriously good.
Cantonese-American cooking with a Brooklyn wit — nostalgic and inventive at once.
Bright, all-day Mexican cooking from the Cosme team — fresh, light, and always buzzing.
Wood-fired, one-star Mexican cooking in a sunlit Greenpoint room.
A Chinatown stalwart doing precise, handmade dim sum — credentialed and beloved.
Shanghainese home cooking done with real care — a Bib-listed crowd favourite.
Five thousand years of art in one building on Fifth Avenue — do the Temple of Dendur, the European paintings and the rooftop bar, then let the rest go; it's too big for one day.
Van Gogh's Starry Night, Monet's Water Lilies room, Warhol and Picasso — the modern canon in a light-filled building; go at opening or in the last two hours to dodge the crush.
Frank Lloyd Wright's white spiral is the reason to come as much as the art — take the lift up and walk the ramp down past the Kandinskys.

A steel baron's Fifth Avenue mansion hung with Vermeer, Rembrandt and Bellini — reopened April 2025 after a $220m restoration that finally opened the family's upstairs rooms to the public; the most civilised hour of art in the city.

venues.n: The Whitney Museum of American Art
venues.d: Renzo Piano's museum of American art at the foot of the High Line — Hopper, O'Keeffe, Basquiat inside, and terraces that frame the Hudson and downtown skyline for free.

The Met's medieval outpost, built from real French monastery cloisters on a bluff over the Hudson — the Unicorn Tapestries, herb gardens and river views make the subway ride uptown worth it. A quiet gem most visitors miss.
J.P. Morgan's private study and jewel-box library — Gutenberg Bibles, illuminated manuscripts and a domed rotunda in the financier's own home. Small, sumptuous, rarely crowded.

venues.n: The American Museum of Natural History
venues.d: Blue whale, dinosaur halls and the Rose planetarium plus the new Gilder science wing — the single best half-day in the city for children and multi-generational groups.
A small mansion museum for German and Austrian art — home to Klimt's gold Woman in Gold — with Café Sabarsky downstairs for Viennese pastry. A refined pairing of art and Kaffeehaus.
Isamu Noguchi's own studio turned into a museum of stone sculpture around a still garden — a meditative escape a short hop across the river. Pair it with nearby Socrates Sculpture Park.
Two black reflecting pools in the tower footprints and a museum beneath ground zero — sobering and beautifully done; book the museum ahead and allow a quiet couple of hours.

The harbour crossing and the immigration halls are the real experience — book crown or pedestal access weeks ahead through your advisor, as they sell out; families can trace ancestors in the Ellis Island records.
The 86th-floor open-air deck still delivers the classic New York view; the redone second-floor museum is genuinely good. Go at dusk to catch daylight and the lit city in one visit.

venues.n: Top of the Rock, Rockefeller Center
venues.d: The best skyline view precisely because it looks back at the Empire State and up Central Park — three open decks, no glass in your photos. The new 'Beam' rooftop experience is a fun add-on.

venues.a: Midtown East / next to Grand Central
venues.d: The most theatrical observation deck — mirrored rooms, glass-floor ledges over Madison Avenue and glass 'Ascent' lifts on the building's flank; part art installation, part view. Book a timed slot.

The Western Hemisphere's highest outdoor sky deck, with an angled glass floor and a lean-out corner over the West Side; adrenaline-seekers can add the 'City Climb' harnessed ascent up the building's exterior.
Top of the tallest tower in the Western Hemisphere — a fast lift with a time-lapse of the city's rise, then harbour-to-Manhattan views. Best paired with the 9/11 Memorial below.
The best free thing in New York — a 25-minute ride past the Statue of Liberty and the downtown skyline, no ticket, no queue. Ride out, turn around, ride back; go at golden hour.
The 843-acre green heart of the city — the Bethesda Terrace, the Ramble, the Bow Bridge and the Reservoir loop; hire bikes or a rowboat, or take the kids to the zoo. A different world every season.
A disused elevated freight line turned wild-planted walkway above the West Side, threading past galleries and river views; walk it end to end and step off into Chelsea's art scene or Hudson Yards.

A pocket park floating over the Hudson on concrete 'tulips' by Heatherwick — undulating lawns, hidden overlooks and a small amphitheatre with summer performances. Free, and a lovely 20 minutes off the High Line.
Walk the elevated wooden promenade from Manhattan into Brooklyn for the definitive skyline view; go early morning to have the cathedral-like stone arches nearly to yourself, then descend into DUMBO.

Cobbled streets under the bridge, the Instagram-famous Washington Street view of the Manhattan Bridge, Jane's Carousel and a green waterfront that faces the whole downtown skyline. End the bridge walk here.
The marble arch, the fountain, the chess players and street musicians — the bohemian soul of the city, ringed by NYU and low townhouse streets perfect for aimless wandering.

Crooked, tree-lined streets of red-brick townhouses, tiny bookshops and cafés — the prettiest walk in Manhattan and the loveliest for an unhurried morning. Bleecker and Perry streets are the postcard.
The world's densest run of cast-iron architecture, now a cobblestoned luxury shopping quarter — flagship boutiques below, ornate 19th-century facades above. Look up as much as into the windows.
One of the largest Chinese communities in the West — dim sum, tea shops and produce markets flowing into the last blocks of Little Italy on Mulberry Street; a sensory wander best done hungry.

The old immigrant tenement district turned gallery-and-cocktail neighbourhood; the Tenement Museum tells the story through restored apartments, then the streets deliver vintage shops and the New Museum.
The capital of Black American culture — a Sunday gospel service, the Apollo Theater, soul food on Lenox Avenue and the Studio Museum; take a guided walk to read the history in the brownstones.
Brooklyn's design-and-nightlife capital — independent boutiques, rooftop bars and the best Manhattan-skyline sunset in the city from the East River waterfront. Take the ferry over for the arrival.
The stage where Ella Fitzgerald, James Brown and Aretha were made — catch the legendary Amateur Night or a show, or take the daytime tour of a true American music landmark.

The world's benchmark for musical theatre — book a marquee show months ahead through your advisor; family groups can't go wrong with The Lion King or Aladdin. Skip Times Square itself once you've seen it.

venues.n: Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts
venues.d: The Metropolitan Opera, the New York Philharmonic and City Ballet around a floodlit travertine plaza and fountain — dress up for a Met Opera night, one of the great evenings out in the city.
The most storied concert hall in America, with acoustics musicians travel the world to play — a recital here is a bucket-list evening; a backstage tour reveals the history if you can't catch a show.

venues.n: Village Vanguard & the Village jazz clubs
venues.d: The basement room where Coltrane and Bill Evans recorded live albums — still the holy ground of jazz. Book the early set; pair it with Blue Note or Smalls nearby for a proper night of music.
Not a station so much as a Beaux-Arts cathedral — the celestial-ceiling main concourse, the Whispering Gallery and an oyster bar in the vaults below. Free, always open, and quietly astonishing.

venues.n: The New York Public Library (Stephen A. Schwarzman Building)
venues.d: The marble-lion library whose Rose Reading Room — a football-field of chandeliers and painted clouds — is open to anyone who walks in; catch a free treasures exhibition and step next door into Bryant Park.
An Art Deco city-within-a-city — the golden Prometheus and the sunken plaza (ice-skating in winter, the giant tree in December), Radio City next door and Top of the Rock above. The heart of Midtown.
The great white Gothic-Revival cathedral facing Rockefeller Center — step in from the Fifth Avenue bustle for the soaring nave and rose window; a five-minute pause that resets the whole day.

Calatrava's soaring white-ribbed transit hall — like a bird or a whale's skeleton in marble — now a luxury shopping concourse; the most dramatic piece of new architecture downtown, and free to walk through.

The world's densest concentration of contemporary art galleries — Gagosian, David Zwirner, Hauser & Wirth and dozens more, all free to enter. Spend a Saturday afternoon drifting between shows off the High Line.

A former Nabisco biscuit factory turned covered food hall — lobster, tacos, artisan pastry and design shops in brick-and-pipe arcades; graze your way through, then step straight onto the High Line above.

venues.n: Grand Central Market & Great Northern Food Hall
venues.d: Within and beside the terminal — a European-style market of cheese, seafood and fresh bread, and Nordic food stalls under the arches. A civilised graze while you admire the building.

America's largest open-air food market — a hundred-odd vendors of everything from ramen burgers to mango sticky rice, with the Manhattan skyline behind. Weekends only, and a great way to eat your way through Brooklyn.

The full spectrum of luxury — the marquee flagships and Bergdorf Goodman on Fifth, the quieter European maisons and galleries up Madison. Your advisor can arrange private appointments and after-hours access.

The most stylish shopping in the city — flagship fashion, concept stores and independent design along cast-iron blocks; less crowded and more curated than Fifth Avenue, and made for wandering on foot.

venues.n: A Central Park bike or pedicab ride
venues.d: The loveliest way to see the whole park in an hour — hire bikes at Columbus Circle, or take a guided pedicab to the film locations and hidden corners. Gentler and more private than the carriage horses.

Board a classic schooner or private yacht for a sail past the Statue of Liberty as the skyline lights up — the single most romantic hour in New York, and easily chartered privately through your advisor.
Fifteen minutes over the harbour, the Statue of Liberty and the length of the skyline — the view that puts the whole city in one frame; ask your advisor about doors-off or private charters.
A commuter aerial cable-car — on a subway swipe — that glides over the East River beside the Queensboro Bridge for a five-minute skyline ride; a quiet thrill most visitors never find.

venues.n: Prospect Park & the Brooklyn Botanic Garden
venues.d: The same designers' 'better' park than Central Park — meadows, a lake and a ravine with fewer crowds — beside a botanic garden famed for its spring cherry blossom and Japanese pond. A perfect Brooklyn morning.

A 478-acre Victorian garden cemetery of rolling hills, glacial ponds and Gothic gates — resting place of Basquiat and Bernstein, with the best hidden harbour view in Brooklyn. Wildly atmospheric and almost empty.

venues.n: The Cathedral of St. John the Divine
venues.d: The largest Gothic cathedral in the world, still famously unfinished — a vast, cool, half-built nave with a peacock in the close. Deeply atmospheric, and paired well with a Columbia University stroll.

Restored immigrant apartments in a preserved 1863 tenement, told through the real families who lived there — the most moving history lesson in the city, and resonant for anyone whose own family emigrated. Book a tour ahead.

A 500-acre open-air sculpture park where monumental Calders, Serras and Goldsworthys sit in rolling meadows and woods — a full day of art and landscape; hire bikes on arrival. A superb warm-weather day trip.

The summer-weekend playground of Manhattan's elite — ocean beaches, hedge-lined estates, farm stands and East Hampton village; best mid-week to avoid the crowds. Your advisor can arrange a house or a beach club.
The most beautiful bar in New York — Ludwig Bemelmans' murals, a grand piano, a perfect martini.
A former World's Best Bar reviving the lost art of the New York-Irish tavern.
A Japanese-American izakaya bar that has ranked among the world's best for years.
Cocktails on the 64th floor with a 360-degree sweep of the harbour and the skyline.
An inventive back-room bar that was recently ranked the best in North America.
The birthplace of the Bloody Mary, beneath Maxfield Parrish's mural — old-money New York.
A no-menu speakeasy where you name a spirit and a mood — bespoke drinks, no fuss.
A theatrical cocktail laboratory high in the Mandarin Oriental — drinks as edible art.
A speakeasy that helped start the modern cocktail revival — buzzy well past midnight.
Drinks and skyline views by the Brooklyn Bridge — the river breeze on a summer night.
